title: The Race the Tests Passed: Forcing an Interleaving Instead of Hoping for One

questions.question: A race has a window of a few instructions. A test runs the racy code with two real threads 100 times and passes. What can you conclude?
options: Very little: measured at about 0.07 percent of trials stranding a task, a suite that runs it 100 times passes with the bug in about 93 percent of the time
That 100 trials is enough
The code is safe
The code is racy
questions.explanation: The buggy version stranded a task in 2 to 28 of 20000 trials depending on the run, and the fixed one in 0 of 180000. A clean run proves nothing, which lessons 07-01 and 07-09 measured twice already.

questions.question: submit counts a task under the lock, releases it, and pushes under the lock again. Shutdown runs in the gap between. What happens, and why?
options: Nothing, since both halves are locked
shutdown waits for the push
The push is refused
The task is pushed into a queue shutdown has already drained
questions.explanation: It is accepted and counted and never processed: stranded. Every access is locked and the whole is not atomic. It is the check-then-act race. The fix is one lock held across the check and the push.

questions.question: A hook at submit.gap runs shutdown() on the same thread as the submit. What did the buggy version do across 300 trials, and what did running two real threads 300 times do?
options: The unaided run found it 300 times
The forced hook stranded a task in 300 of 300, where the unaided run usually found 0 in 300
The forced hook found nothing
Both stranded a task in every trial
questions.explanation: No timing is involved, so the failure is the same every time. Forcing the interleaving needs no second thread and no luck. The unaided count varies between 0 and a handful and is printed and not asserted.

questions.question: Shutdown is injected at each point of one submit: before, in the gap, after. For the buggy intake, how many strand a task?
options: All three
None
Before and after, not the gap
Only the gap: before, the submit is refused; after, shutdown finds the task already queued and drains it
questions.explanation: Three places shutdown can run, two harmless and one not. The fixed version has no gap, so that hook never fires. Trying every point is a small exhaustive search of the interleavings of two steps.

questions.question: A race point is placed inside a locked section, and the hook calls an operation that takes the same lock. What happens, measured?
options: It works, since the hook runs later
It throws
It hangs: one thread locking a std::mutex it holds waits for itself, and a 3 second timeout killed the program
It deadlocks only on Windows
questions.explanation: Place points where no lock is held, and have hooks call the public operations. race_point also copies the action out and runs it after releasing its own table lock, for the same reason.

questions.question: What does a race point cost when no hook is installed?
options: A mutex lock and a table search
A function call through std::function
One atomic load that finds the installed count at zero, and a return, which is why it can stay in production code
Nothing, it is compiled out
questions.explanation: hooks_installed() is atomic so the common case never takes the table's mutex. The suite checks that with nothing installed the point does nothing, and that it goes back to doing nothing when a hook is removed.
